Question:
Steph scored \(15\) baskets out of \(20\) attempts in the first half of a game, and \(10\) baskets out of \(10\) attempts in the second half. Candace took \(12\) attempts in the first half and \(18\) attempts in the second. In each half, Steph scored a higher percentage of baskets than Candace. Surprisingly they ended with the same overall percentage of baskets scored. How many more baskets did Candace score in the second half than in the first?

[Figure 1](figures/2022_AMC_8_Q21_question_fig1.svg)
Solution:
Both players attempted \(30\) shots. Steph made \(15+10=25\), so matching Steph's overall percentage means Candace also made \(25\).

In the first half, Steph made \(15/20=3/4\) of the shots. Candace's percentage was lower, so Candace made fewer than \((3/4)\cdot12=9\) baskets, hence at most \(8\).

In the second half, Steph made every shot. Candace's percentage was again lower, so Candace made at most \(17\) of \(18\).

Those two upper bounds add to \(8+17=25\), exactly the required total. Candace must therefore have made \(8\) and \(17\) baskets. The difference is \(17-8=\boxed{9}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\). The different numbers of attempts explain how the overall percentages can match despite Steph's advantage in both halves.
